A.explanation: This is valid because $P = VI$ rearranges to $I = P/V$, so it cannot be the not-valid relationship.

B.explanation: This is valid because $W = VQ$ for charge $Q$ moved through p.d. $V$ rearranges to $Q = W/V$.

C.explanation: This is valid because $P = I^2 R$ rearranges to $R = P/I^2$.

D.explanation: This is not valid because $R = V/I$ combined with $P = VI$ gives $R = V^2/P$, not $V/P$.

hints: Start from what $V$, $I$, $P$, $W$ and $Q$ mean for the resistor: $P = VI$ links power to current and p.d., and $W = VQ$ links work to charge and p.d.
Combine $P = VI$ with $R = V/I$ to get the two correct power-resistance forms $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$, then rearrange each one.
Test the $R = V/P$ statement with units: $V/P$ has units of $\text{V W}^{-1}$, while resistance in ohms is $\text{V A}^{-1}$, so an extra $V$ is missing.
walkthrough: Recall the defining relations for the resistor: resistance $R = V/I$, power $P = VI$, and work done moving charge $W = VQ$.
Check $I = P/V$: from $P = VI$, divide both sides by $V$ to get $I = P/V$, so this relation is valid.
Check $Q = W/V$: from $W = VQ$, divide both sides by $V$ to get $Q = W/V$, so this relation is valid.
Check $R = P/I^2$: substitute $V = IR$ into $P = VI$ to get $P = I^2R$, then divide by $I^2$ to get $R = P/I^2$, so this relation is valid.
Check $R = V/P$: using $P = VI$ gives $V/P = V/(VI) = 1/I$, which has units of $\text{A}^{-1}$, not ohms, so it cannot equal $R$. The correct form is $R = V^2/P$.
Therefore the only not-valid relationship is $R = V/P$. This is option D.
